I tried to photograph it, but the camera kept focusing on a smudge where my nose had touched the glass. My crewmate Jo says I spend more time at the window than at my experiments. My brother complained about the weather, then went very quiet and gripped the wheel with both hands. Nobody made jokes. Nobody even tried to eat the sandwiches. It took us six hours to get back, a trip that usually takes two. When we finally tied up at the jetty, I sat down on a crate and didn't move for a long time. We didn't catch a single fish, and I have never been so glad to see dry land.

Every evening, at the end of its work, it sent us a photo of the Martian sunset, as if it were saying goodnight to the people who built it. Last week, the dust finally won. Then she pushed off into the shallows, and the water folded itself softly around her shell. A few seconds later, she surfaced once, took a breath and was gone. Nobody on the beach said anything for a while. Then the youngest volunteer, who had fed Crumpet every morning, burst into happy tears. We will miss her, but she is exactly where she belongs.

Training diary, Week 12. Today was the day I'd been dreading since I first signed up: the spinning chair. It's a seat on the end of a long metal arm that whirls you round and round to test how much your body can take before you black out or throw up. The instructor strapped me in and gave me a paper bag, which did not make me feel any better.

The moment the arm started to turn, my stomach dropped about forty floors. After one minute, my cheeks were pulled back so far that I could see my own ears. After two minutes, I'm fairly sure my brain had swapped places with my lunch. The instructor's voice came through the headset, calm and slow, telling me to breathe, but I couldn't remember how breathing worked. Six minutes felt like six hundred years.

When the arm finally stopped, I sat there with my eyes shut while the room kept spinning without me. I didn't need the paper bag, which my instructor said makes me one of only three trainees this year. Tomorrow I have to do it again. I am going to eat a very small breakfast.

frame: Wren wrote about her first night aboard the Soggy Biscuit. The Whiskrel slept through all of it.
text:
My first night aboard the Soggy Biscuit was not what I had imagined. I had pictured myself drifting off to sleep under the stars, rocked gently by the tide, dreaming about the Creatures we would rescue. Instead, Tully pointed me to a narrow bunk below deck, squeezed between a cupboard full of tins and a pile of Gus's experiments, and switched off the only light.

I lay there in the pitch dark with my eyes shut, trying not to think about what might be in the experiments. That was when the boat began to talk. The groan of the old hull timbers and the slap of loose rope against the mast kept me awake for hours. Somewhere near my feet, water gurgled through a pipe. Above me, footsteps creaked across the deck as someone on watch walked from one end to the other and back again. Every few minutes, Mo, in the next bunk, let out a snore like a small motorbike starting up.

At some point I must have fallen asleep, because the next thing I knew, sunlight was pouring through the porthole and Mo was offering me a fried egg on a slice of toast that was, somehow, also wet. I said yes. By the third night, I could sleep through anything.

text:
Nobody had been inside the old fishing shed at the end of the creek for years. From the outside, it looked like it might fall down if someone sneezed. The tin walls were orange with rust, the windows were boarded up, and a crooked sign on the door said KEEP OUT in faded red paint. Jas and her cousin Theo had dared each other all summer, and on the last night of the holidays, they finally squeezed through the gap in the door with one torch between them.

They had only taken five steps when the torch flickered and died. Theo shook it. Nothing. In the total darkness, the shed seemed to wake up. Something dripped steadily, plink, plink, plink, somewhere above their heads. The tin roof ticked and popped as it cooled. Behind them, the door creaked slowly shut. Then, from the far corner, came a scratching sound, followed by a soft, wet shuffle, as if something heavy was dragging itself across the floor towards them. Jas grabbed Theo's sleeve. Neither of them breathed.

Then Theo's phone lit up with a message from his mum, and in its blue glow they saw a very large, very startled pelican waddling across the floor towards them, dragging an old fishing net behind it. The pelican looked at them. They looked at the pelican. All three of them left the shed at the same time.

text:
The Mangrove Moonlight Concert has been running for twelve years, and this year it was the biggest yet, with more than a thousand people squeezed onto the grassy slope of the amphitheatre. The headline act was a five-piece band from the mainland called The Fiddler Crabs, and by the time they walked on stage, the crowd had been waiting on the hill for over an hour.

The moment they started, purple and blue lights swept across the crowd, catching the raised arms and the bubbles drifting up from the front row. The drummer's sticks cracked against the snare like a whip, and the singer's voice soared over the top of it all. Halfway through the second song, a light rain began to fall, but nobody moved. Sweat ran down the back of my neck and soaked my shirt. People stood on the hill singing every word. The smell of popcorn and wet grass drifted up from the stalls behind us.

The band played for nearly two hours and finished with an encore that had the whole hill jumping. Walking back to the ferry afterwards, my ears still buzzing, I decided it was the best concert I have ever been to.

MIRAGE AT DAWN

Before the sun, before the birds,
before the boats begin to stir,
soft, silent, silver, the mist slides in
and wraps the mangroves, root and limb.

It settles slowly on the tide.
It hides the jetty, hides the shore.
The island holds its breath and waits,
as still as it has been before.

Then light: a crack of gold, a gull,
a fisherman who starts his motor.
The mist lifts up and drifts away,
and morning floods across the water.

Pip says the first stanza is the hardest to get right. 'The mist never makes a sound,' she says. 'It creeps in so softly that you only notice it when the jetty has gone.'
